posts.question: What do you say you're bad at so nobody asks you to do it?
posts.caption:
What do you say you're bad at so nobody asks you to do it?

If your answer came fast: who ends up doing it?

“Bad at” is one of the few excuses people accept without a second question: bad at texting back, bad at directions, bad at planning the trip. It is often true, and it also hands the job to someone else for good. The follow-up is about that someone.

posts.question: What did you buy this year for the person you were planning to become?
posts.caption:
What did you buy this year for the person you were planning to become?

If your answer came fast: where is it right now?

The running shoes, the film camera, the cookbook with one stained page. Buying the thing is the fastest part of becoming someone, which is why it gets done first. The follow-up only asks for a location, and the location is usually a closet.

posts.question: Whose opinion of your apartment do you imagine when you clean it?
posts.caption:
Whose opinion of your apartment do you imagine when you clean it?

If your answer came fast: when were they last there?

Most people clean for one specific visitor, and it is rarely whoever is actually coming over. The name tends to arrive before the question ends. The follow-up asks for a date, because that visitor has often not been by in years.

A swipe takes less than a second, which is about how long a rule takes to apply. The second slide asks whether the rule would have removed you, and the third asks what you are hoping gets a longer look. Stop on whichever one you'd rather not answer.

posts.question: What do you say you're bad at so nobody asks you to do it?
answers: Probably. People get less bad at the things they keep doing. This protects you from being seen learning.
They got better by doing it every time you didn't. This protects the arrangement.
The fastest answer of the three. Not complaining and not minding are different things. This protects you from asking which it is.
posts.caption:
Tuesday's question, read back. Three answers that come fast, and what each one tends to protect.

None of them is wrong. The point is which one you reached for first, and who has been doing the thing since.

posts.question: What's the last compliment you talked someone out of?
posts.followup: What would it cost you to believe it?
posts.caption:
What's the last compliment you talked someone out of?

If your answer came fast: what would it cost you to believe it?

“It was nothing,” “I got lucky,” “the team did most of it.” The correction comes out faster than a thank you, and it passes for modesty. The follow-up asks what the compliment would have asked of you if you had let it stand.
